questions.question: In imperative programming, what is meant by a program's state?

choices.statement: The set of syntax rules that the compiler uses to validate the source code
The contents of the program's storage locations (variables) at a given point in its execution, which commands modify
The sequence of logical statements the interpreter must prove true
The final output produced after the program terminates

questions.hint: It is what the variables hold at a given moment.

questions.question: In the assignment statement x = x + 1 , what do the x on the left and the x on the right denote?

choices.statement: Both denote values
Both denote locations
The left x denotes a location and the right x denotes a value
The left x denotes a value and the right x denotes a location

questions.hint: One side is a place to store something; the other side is something to read.

questions.question: Which statement about ALGOL 60 is consistent with the source material?

choices.statement: It introduced BNF notation for defining syntax, along with block structure, structured control statements and recursive procedures, but it failed to win wide acceptance in industry.
It was designed by IBM for business data processing and became the dominant language for banking systems.
It was a direct one-to-one transliteration of machine code, with each statement matching one CPU instruction.
It was designed for the IBM 704 and was the first high-level language with floating-point support.

questions.hint: Think of its lasting influence on syntax notation and block structure.

questions.question: Why does the text warn against reading an imperative statement such as a = b as a mathematical statement of equality?

choices.statement: Because assignment is commutative, so a = b and b = a mean the same thing in both settings
Because in Java the = symbol can only be used with constants, never with variables
Because in mathematics an equality is always true once stated, while an assignment only makes two variables equal at that moment and they need not stay equal afterwards
Because an assignment statement can never make two variables hold the same value

questions.hint: An assignment happens once at that moment; equality in math always holds.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the while loop from the do-while loop?

choices.statement: The while loop evaluates its Boolean expression at the end of each iteration, so its body always runs at least once.
The do-while loop evaluates its Boolean expression at the end of each iteration, so its body always runs at least once.
Both loops evaluate their expression only after the body, but do-while can be infinite.
The while loop can be infinite, while the do-while loop is guaranteed to terminate.

questions.hint: One of them checks its condition after running the body.

questions.question: Which description best captures the core idea of declarative programming?

choices.statement: Programs list explicit step-by-step commands that modify a stored state
Programs must be written in a low-level language that maps directly to machine instructions
Programs can only be written using the goto command and sequencing
Programs describe what computation should be performed rather than how to perform it, minimizing or eliminating side effects

questions.hint: Say what you want, not how to get it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a logic variable in logic programming, in contrast to a variable in an imperative language?

choices.statement: Once bound to a term, the binding cannot be destroyed or replaced by a binding to a different constant, although the bound term may be made more specific through other variables
It can be reassigned any number of times, just like an imperative variable
It always holds a fully defined value at the moment it is created
Its bindings are one-directional, so a bound variable can never influence other variables

questions.hint: Once a logic variable is bound, it cannot simply be overwritten.

questions.question: Which set of rules correctly describes the unification algorithm for Prolog as presented in the source material?

choices.statement: A constant unifies with any constant; an uninstantiated variable unifies only with other variables; a structured term unifies with any other structured term

A constant unifies only with itself; an uninstantiated variable unifies with anything and becomes instantiated to it; a structured term unifies with another only if it has the same function name and number of arguments and the arguments unify recursively
A constant unifies only with variables; an instantiated variable can be rebound freely; a structured term unifies with another if they have the same number of arguments, regardless of function name
Unification evaluates arithmetic terms first and succeeds whenever both sides have the same numeric value

questions.hint: Constants only match themselves; variables can take on whatever they meet.

questions.question: According to the source material, which statement correctly describes how Prolog searches for solutions and what the cut operator does?

choices.statement: Prolog uses a breadth-first strategy, and the cut forces it to explore all branches in parallel
Prolog resolves goals right to left and tries clauses bottom to top, and the cut restarts the search from the root
Prolog resolves goals left to right, tries clauses top to bottom in a depth-first search, and backtracks on failure; the cut freezes a choice and prunes the remaining sibling branches to its right
Prolog selects clauses at random, and the cut guarantees that every possible solution is found

questions.hint: Prolog works top to bottom, left to right, and backs up when it gets stuck.

questions.question: Which statement about the functional sub-paradigm of declarative programming is consistent with the source material?

choices.statement: It is rooted in lambda calculus, a mathematical abstraction (not a programming language) used to study computability, function definition, function application and recursion, and it forms the basis of almost all functional languages
It is rooted in first-order predicate calculus and relies on automatic backtracking as its only control mechanism
It was created as a direct abstraction of the Turing machine and the Von Neumann machine with a modifiable store
It is a markup-based approach such as HTML, in which tags describe the visual rendering of a page

questions.hint: Its roots are in a mathematical abstraction from the 1930s, not a programming language.

questions.question:
What is the result of the following Prolog query?

sum_to(0, 0).
sum_to(N, S) :-
    N > 0,
    N1 is N - 1,
    sum_to(N1, S1),
    S is S1 + N.

?- sum_to(4, X).

choices.statement: false.

questions.hint: sum_to adds N + (N-1) + ... + 0.

bird(tweety).
bird(polly).

bird(tweety).
bird(polly).

bird(polly).

number(4).

number(2).
number(4).

number(4).

questions.question:
Which clause completes the program to calculate the sum from 1 to N?

Expected query and result:
?- sum_to(3, X).
X = 6.

sum_to(0, 0).
sum_to(N, S) :-
    N > 0,
    N1 is N - 1,
    sum_to(N1, S1),
    __________

choices.statement: S is S1 + N.
S is S1 * N.
S is S1 - N.
S is N - S1.

questions.hint: Add the current N to the sum of the smaller numbers.

questions.question:
Which clause completes the program so that it counts the elements of a list?

Expected query and result:
?- list_length([a,b,c], N).
N = 3.

list_length([], 0).
list_length([_|Tail], N) :-
    list_length(Tail, N1),
    __________

choices.statement: N is N1 - 1.
N is N1 + 1.
N = N1.
N is N1 * 2.

questions.hint: The length is one more than the length of the tail.
